title: Gulab Jamun Macarons at 35,000 Feet: Air India's New SFO Maharaja Lounge Is a Love Letter to NRI Food Culture
excerpt: The airline's first branded U.S. lounge serves dal Bukhara, motichoor cheesecake bites, and hot parathas off the griddle — rewriting the rules of airport dining for the diaspora.
body:
For decades, the NRI travel experience has had a familiar rhythm: endure a mediocre American airport lounge, board a long-haul flight, and wait until landing in India for food that actually tastes like home. Air India's new Maharaja Lounge at San Francisco International Airport is trying to break that pattern — and the menu is the reason to pay attention.

## Dal Bukhara Before Departure

The lounge, which opened this month in SFO's Concourse A, serves a rotating menu of Indian and international dishes from a full dining room designed to feel more like a restaurant than a typical airport buffet line.

During its opening week, the spread leaned heavily into Indian comfort food: dal Bukhara, chicken tikka masala, vegetable biryani, paneer moringa, and beet-and-fig sham savera kofta sat alongside grilled salmon and vegetables. A cold spread featured house specialty dips including tikka achari and mango habanero. Smaller bites ranged from fish croquettes to paneer in Szechuan sauce.

But the real headlines are the desserts. Air India has developed modernized takes on Indian classics, including gulab jamun macarons, motichoor cheesecake bites, and a reimagined gajar ka halwa served in a tart-like bite-sized presentation. For breakfast, hot parathas come straight off the griddle.

## The Emotional Architecture

The Maharaja Lounge is not just a food story — it is a design statement. The interiors blend champagne, ivory, and deep red tones aligned with Air India's evolving brand identity. A speakeasy-inspired Aviator's Bar offers a curated cocktail list that includes the Maharaja Manhattan, crafted with Indian black pepper as a reinterpretation of the classic.

Art installations by local artists showcase regional Indian heritage, while selected displays incorporate upcycled aircraft components transformed into contemporary art pieces. The space is divided into a Social Zone for communal interaction, a Business Class section overlooking the tarmac, and a Private Zone for First Class passengers seeking quiet.

The lounge operates daily from 6 AM until just before midnight — far beyond Air India's own departure bank — and is accessible to First and Business Class passengers on Air India and other Star Alliance carriers.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For the tens of thousands of Indian Americans who fly between the Bay Area and India every year, the Maharaja Lounge addresses something that sounds trivial but is not: the emotional transition between two worlds.

The best airport lounges understand that travel is stressful and that food is comfort. For NRIs, that comfort has specific parameters — it is dal Bukhara and paratha and chai, not another Caesar salad and a mediocre Chardonnay. By putting Indian cuisine at the center of a premium lounge experience at one of the country's busiest airports for India-bound flights, Air India is acknowledging what the diaspora has always known: the journey home begins with the first bite, not the first boarding call.

## What's Next

The SFO lounge is part of Air India's broader transformation under the Tata Group, which reacquired the airline in 2022. The emphasis on food as a brand differentiator — not just onboard, but on the ground — suggests more such lounges may follow at other major hubs with heavy India traffic. For NRI travelers who have spent years making do with United Polaris salads, the Maharaja Lounge is a quiet revolution.
author: Diaspora Desk
